Commission guide

Dressmaker Customer Preferences

Customer preferences in Dressmaker are not a hidden stat sheet. The developers have published no client roster, no preference score and no table of who wants which lace. What you get is a brief: an occasion, a person with their own taste, and a dress to make.

Reviewed September 21, 2026

  • What a brief hasOccasion, taste, budget, targets
  • Targets are numericQuality 70, Flowers 60, Cute 30, Romantic 45
  • Limits tooQuality 0/80, Formal 0/50, Simple 0/75
  • Hard rules existSome briefs say "use only black"
  • RewardCoin, reputation and a star rating
  • Second incomeOff-rack dresses in the shop window

Every commission carries a written brief with named attribute targets — one official example reads Quality 70, Flowers 60, Cute 30, Romantic 45 — plus an occasion and a budget. Meet them and you gain coin and reputation; ignore the brief and the reaction tells you so. The developers have never published a customer roster or how the star rating is calculated.

Quick reference

What a brief containsWhere you see itExample
The occasionThe customer's note, in the sketchbookA wedding, a formal evening, everyday wear
Their tasteThe same note, in their own words"Something soft", "not too much fuss"
Attribute targetsSketchbook, Requirements boxQuality 70, Flowers 60, Cute 30, Romantic 45
Commission limitsFabric shopQuality 0/80, Formal 0/50, Simple 0/75, Professional 0/50
A budgetSketchbook, beside the requirements800, and roughly 3.85m of fabric
Hard rulesFabric shop, as a constraint line"Use only black"

The developers publish no client roster and no preference score, so the rest is your read of the person. New here? Start with the dressmaker game overview.

Occasion first, taste second

Build for the occasion and let taste decide the details: print is a choice on a guest's dress and a mistake against a bride. In your window you choose the brief; in a commission, it chooses you.

  • The one big day

    A wedding or formal event that forgives nothing: best cloth, restrained decoration, a practice run in cheap fabric.

  • The dress that has to keep working

    Everyday wear, where wearability beats drama.

  • The open brief

    "Make me something lovely." No plan, so the customer reacts to the dress itself.

Reading taste signals

Customers rarely say what they want precisely, and some of the signals are not words.

SignalWhat to listen forWhat to do
Colour language"Something soft" against "something cheerful"Attitude, not hue: two different dresses from matching swatches
Adjectives"Elegant" against "fun"Restraint means cleaner lines; permission means decorate
HesitationA customer who goes quiet when you suggest somethingA soft no: offer a second option, and never design from a paused suggestion
The shop windowWhich finished dress they drift toward while they talkA free focus group, harder to fake than a request

Turning a vague brief into choices

Find the closest row below and start there.

Note

the attribute names below are the game's, taken from the Requirements box it shows you. Turning vague brief language into those attributes is our framework, not official documentation.

What the customer saysSilhouetteFabricColourTrim
"Something like the one in your window"Close to the display, simplifiedSame family as the displayWhat they saw, softerAlmost none
"Whatever you think looks best"Your plainest flattering shapeCloth you have sewn beforeA colour that suits themOne accent
"It is for a wedding"Formal and structuredThe best cloth you can cut twiceQuiet beside the coupleFine lace, no jokes
"I do not want to stand out"Familiar, easy to move inMatte and forgivingMuted, near what they wearDetail at the edges
"I love this colour" (hand on a bolt)Whatever shows the cloth offThat exact fabric, if affordableTheir pick; build around itEchoing trim

The safe answer is usually the polite one.

How the reward loop works

Hand a finished dress over and you are paid twice: coin buys fabric, reputation buys the future. The official bullet list says you "turn in dresses to customers to gain reputation and coin."

You giveYou getRisk
A dress that meets the briefCoin, reputation and a good star ratingOnly the fabric you spent
A dress that misses the briefLess coin, and you see it in the reactionA miss builds no standing
A sabotaged dressThe reaction you were fishing forCosts the standing that unlocks better work
A dress sold off the rackSteady coin, on a brief you choseLow: nobody is waiting on it

Reputation thresholds are unpublished. Off-rack dresses are the steadier half of the economy, with roughly 35 hours of story commissions besides.

Playing the sabotage run on purpose

The official Steam page invites you to "satisfy (or sabotage!)" the townsfolk. The feedback is a person, not a scoreboard.

  1. 1

    Miss the occasion

    send something theatrical to the customer who asked for everyday wear.

  2. 2

    Ignore stated taste

    they told you no pink, so every panel is pink.

  3. 3

    Clash fabric and trim

    heavy velvet under delicate lace, or lace on lace until it stops reading as a dress.

  4. 4

    Decorate past the point of sense

    buttons, bows and appliqué "wherever you like" is the official promise, and the freedom that ruins a silhouette.

Warning

the joke costs reputation. A sabotaged dress does not build the standing that unlocks better work, so spend it when reputation is not scarce — after the story gives you a cushion.

Recovering from a bad commission

If you have just handed over a disaster, do not restart.

  1. 1

    Practise on the cheapest cloth

    remake the dress in fabric nobody will wear; you are training your eye, not producing a garment.

  2. 2

    Take the plain commissions

    an easy dress handed in well beats a risky one handed in badly.

  3. 3

    Give the miss a second life

    sell it off the rack, so a dress wrong for one brief still earns back part of its fabric.

Keep the sketchbook entry: a dress that failed on colour and trim usually had a fine silhouette.

Frequently asked questions

  1. How many customers are in Dressmaker?

    The developers have not published a customer count or any names. The store page promises "a whole town of people."

  2. Is there a score or a star rating for a dress?

    Partly. A turn-in gives you coin and reputation, and the customer card shows a star rating — one official screenshot shows five stars with only one lit. How those stars are worked out has never been published.

  3. Do customers remember a bad dress?

    We cannot verify how the town tracks past commissions. Reputation is the standing currency, so a bad turn-in is a slow cost, not a permanent ban.

  4. What is the fastest way to build reputation?

    Match the occasion and the stated taste, and turn dresses in often. No shortcut or coin-bought standing has been published.
